title: Queen Windmill
summary: Promote after offering the bishop, then circle that bishop with forcing queen checks until the opposing queen is skewered.

nodes.question: Can the bishop help after both sides promote?
nodes.explanation: White has Ke8, Bc8 and c7 against Ke5, a3 and b3. The bishop appears to obstruct the pawn, but can become a shield around which the new queen checks.

branches.title: Circle the bishop and skewer the queen
commentary: White has Ke8, Bc8 and c7 against Ke5, a3 and b3. The bishop appears to obstruct the pawn, but can become a shield around which the new queen checks.
Bf5 vacates c8 and offers itself to the black king. The bishop also covers d3/e4/g4/h3 for the upcoming checks.
a2 declines the bishop and creates an immediate promotion threat.
c8=Q promotes first. White needs the bishop to make progress after Black also promotes.
a1=Q gets Black a queen and seems to balance the material, but the exposed king becomes the tactical target.
Qe6+ checks vertically and begins the circuit around Bf5.
Kf4 hides below the bishop in the illustrated defense.
Qe4+ checks across the fourth rank and changes which king flights remain.
Kg5 moves to the bishop’s right, continuing to hide near it rather than retreating to the lower board.
Qg4+ checks up the g-file and forces another change of side.
Kf6 moves above the bishop in the selected line.
Qg6+ checks along the sixth rank, continuing the queen’s circuit.
Ke5 reaches the same diagonal as Qa1: a1-b2-c3-d4-e5-f6-g7.
Qg7+ skewers the king against the queen on a1. Black cannot save both targets in this selected line.
Kxf5 finally captures the bishop, escaping check but uncovering the diagonal.
Qxa1 takes the queen. White’s queen against Kf5 and the remaining b3 pawn is an exact tablebase win, not an assertion of immediate mate.
branches.explanation: Qxa1 takes the queen. White’s queen against Kf5 and the remaining b3 pawn is an exact tablebase win, not an assertion of immediate mate.

branches.title: Take the bishop immediately
commentary: White has Ke8, Bc8 and c7 against Ke5, a3 and b3. The bishop appears to obstruct the pawn, but can become a shield around which the new queen checks.
Bf5 clears c8 while placing the bishop where the king can capture it.
Kxf5 takes the offered bishop, but now c8 promotes with check on the c8-d7-e6-f5 diagonal.
c8=Q+ promotes with tempo. The exact queen-versus-two-pawns position is winning; White has time to address the advancing pawns.
branches.explanation: c8=Q+ promotes with tempo. The exact queen-versus-two-pawns position is winning; White has time to address the advancing pawns.

branches.title: Independent diagonal retreat comparison
commentary: An independent representative reply demonstrates why a king retreat onto the a1 diagonal exposes the black queen even sooner.
Bf5 prepares promotion while offering the bishop.
a2 advances the outside pawn instead of capturing.
c8=Q clears the promotion race on White’s side.
a1=Q creates the target on the long diagonal.
Qe6+ forces the king to choose a flight.
Kd4 steps onto the diagonal to Qa1. This is a selected independent alternative, not an exhaustive account of king replies.
Qf6+ skewers the king against Qa1 along f6-e5-d4-c3-b2-a1, while staying out of the king’s capture range.
Kc4 is a representative legal escape from the check.
Qxa1 captures the queen while preserving the bishop. The resulting position is checked as a White win.

branches.explanation: Qxa1 captures the queen while preserving the bishop. The resulting position is checked as a White win.

exercises.prompt: What role does the bishop play after promotion?
exercises.answer: It restricts the king’s flights while the queen changes checking lines around it. The selected circuit finally puts king and queen on one diagonal, enabling a skewer.

startContext: The full six-piece physical-board diagram is reconstructed from saved board images and the Bf5/c8 promotion anchors. The source’s full alternative mating tree is not claimed.
